notes.meaning: God calls all the descendants of Jacob to pay close attention to His message. He reminds them that He was the one who rescued their entire family from slavery in Egypt. Because the Lord showed them such great love in the past, their rebellion against Him is especially wrongful and without excuse.

The Lord chose Israel out of all the nations on earth to have a close, loving relationship with Him. With this special privilege came great responsibility to live righteously. Because Israel knew God's will and still chose to disobey, God promised to hold them strictly accountable and punish all their sins.

Two travelers do not walk along a road together unless they first meet and agree on the direction. In the same way, the people of Israel could not expect God to walk with them as a friend while they lived in open disobedience. True fellowship with God requires that our hearts and choices agree with His holy ways.

differ.view: Some in this tradition understand the two travelers to be God and His prophet, showing that Amos only speaks because he is walking in complete agreement with God's call.

notes.meaning: A lion roars in the wild when it spots its prey, and a young lion growls when it has captured its food. Amos uses this picture from nature to show that God does not speak empty threats without a reason. The Lord's warning of judgment is sounding because Israel's wicked choices have made the nation the target of His righteous anger.

A bird does not fall into a net unless a trap was set, and a trap does not snap shut without catching something. These pictures remind the people that national disasters do not happen by pure accident or luck. God's judgments are purposeful, and unrepented sin always brings certain consequences.

When a watchman blows a ram's horn in a city, the people naturally tremble because an invading army is near. In the same way, Israel should take alarm at the prophet's warnings of coming ruin. The disaster mentioned here refers to painful calamity and punishment for sin, showing that the Lord is the one who brings judgment upon a guilty city.

God does not send judgment on His people without first warning them through His prophets. He reveals His plans to His faithful servants so the people have every opportunity to turn away from their evil ways and seek mercy. Israel could never complain that God struck them without plenty of notice.

differ.view: Believers in this tradition emphasize that this statement describes God's specific mercy in warning covenant Israel of impending judgment, rather than a universal rule that God must reveal every single thing He ever does beforehand.

notes.meaning: Just as hearing a lion roar fills anyone with fear, hearing the Lord speak compels the prophet to deliver His message. Amos could not keep quiet because the sovereign God had given him an urgent message to proclaim. The people had no right to blame the prophet for simply obeying his Lord.

The Lord calls pagan neighbors like Philistia and Egypt to gather on the hills surrounding Samaria, the capital city of northern Israel. From these heights, they could look down and witness the widespread violence, chaos, and mistreatment of the weak inside the city. It was deeply shameful that heathen nations were invited to witness how corrupt God's own people had become.

The rulers and wealthy leaders of Samaria had completely lost touch with what was right. Instead of storing up good and honest deeds, their mansions were filled with riches taken by violence and cruelty against the poor. Habitual greed had blinded their consciences to God's standards of justice.

Because of this nonstop oppression, God announced that an enemy nation would soon surround the land. This attacker, which was the superpower Assyria, would tear down Israel's military fortresses and strip away its false confidence. The grand palaces filled with stolen goods would be looted and left in ruins.

A shepherd might pull two leg bones or a scrap of an ear out of a lion's mouth, but only to prove to the owner that the sheep was torn to pieces. In the same way, Samaria's rescue would not be a victory, but a scene of almost total destruction. The wealthy people who lounged on luxurious couches would escape with next to nothing.

The Lord commands His witnesses to testify against the descendants of Jacob. The warning comes from the Lord God of Hosts, a title that means the Commander of all the armies in heaven and earth. Because He possesses all authority, His decree against Israel's rebellion cannot be stopped.

When the day of punishment arrives, the Lord will destroy the altars at Bethel, where Israel practiced false worship with golden calves. The raised corners, called horns, were considered the holiest part of the altar and a place where people fled for safety. God would snap those horns off, proving that false religion cannot protect anyone from His judgment.

God declared that He would tear down both the winter homes and summer houses belonging to the rich ruling class. The grand mansions decorated with expensive ivory panels would be totally destroyed. All the luxury bought with money taken from the poor would vanish in the coming invasion.
